video_title: Megaprojects: Some Assembly Required w/ Ian MacGregor
gist: Alberta industrialist Ian MacGregor, who built the ~$12-13B Northwest Upgrading Sturgeon Refinery, explains why megaprojects always blow their budgets, why private companies structurally can't finance them without government backing, and how a catastrophic gasifier-burner failure (40 hours vs a designed ~2,000) was fixed in-house in 279 days.

themes.theme: Why Megaprojects Always Blow Their Budgets

insights.claim: Ian MacGregor reviewed roughly $150 billion worth of past megaprojects and found every single one came in over its original cost estimate, with his own ~$12 billion Sturgeon Refinery finishing about 69% over budget.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Treat any published megaproject budget as a floor, not a target — historically zero exceptions in a $150B sample set, so investors/analysts should default to expecting overruns of 50-100%+ rather than modeling to the initial estimate.
insights.quote: I went back and I looked at 150 billion dollars of different mega projects. Everyone was over. Uh the best one I think was 69% over. And we were in that group.

insights.claim: MacGregor cites the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion as the worst megaproject overrun he found, coming in at roughly 500% (five times) over its original cost estimate.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A named, extreme benchmark (5x) for tail-risk cost overruns on Canadian energy infrastructure — useful as an upper bound when stress-testing project finance assumptions.
insights.quote: The worst one that I found was Trans Mountain. It was five times over 500% over the original positive estimate.

insights.claim: MacGregor identifies three structural causes of megaproject overruns: (1) even a huge upfront engineering spend (his project spent roughly $100 million on the initial estimate) is never enough to truly understand a first-of-a-kind project, so early cost estimates are inherently low-quality; (2) with thousands of custom equipment pieces feeding a rigid modular construction sequence, late parts get force-installed into an already-built structure at huge extra cost and time; and (3) a single megaproject competing for all local skilled tradespeople exhausts the regional labor pool, forcing recruitment of unproductive imported labor.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A reusable diagnostic checklist for underwriting megaproject risk: check estimate maturity, equipment/module sequencing risk, and local labor-market saturation before trusting a project's schedule or budget.
insights.quote: You have a bad estimate, bad expediting, and poor productivity. And there isn't a hell of a lot you can do about it. Once you press the go button on this baby, you're stuck.

insights.claim: MacGregor argues private companies structurally cannot finance true megaprojects because standard discounted cash flow (e.g., a 10-year PV10 payback target) massively undervalues the long tail of cash flows from assets that will actually operate for 100 years, so only government — the one entity guaranteed to still exist when that tail value arrives — can rationally back them.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Explains why nation-building infrastructure (refineries, rail, SMRs) systematically under-attracts private capital regardless of its true lifetime returns — a structural case for public equity/backstops in capital-intensive, long-lived energy and industrial assets.
insights.quote: These assets last for a hundred years. So what you should be interested in is the tail. But no one running a private company is going to be here when the tail comes in. The only organization that's going to be here for sure is the government.

insights.claim: MacGregor describes a private-sector career-risk mechanism blocking megaprojects: a senior executive's tenure (roughly 6-8 years) closely matches the multi-year window (years 4-8) when a megaproject's worst problems typically surface, so a rational executive avoids sponsoring one because the pain would land on their own watch for a payoff they'd never personally capture.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A concrete incentive-structure explanation for why capable, well-funded private firms keep passing on high-return but high-risk nation-scale projects — a factor to weigh when assessing whether a private sponsor will actually see a megaproject through.
insights.quote: Sounds like all the troubles are going to be occurring on this thing when I'm reaching the end of my career. I don't think I want to sign up for that.

insights.claim: MacGregor uses the original Canadian Pacific Railway as historical proof of the megaproject tail-value thesis: its cost estimate rose from about $25 million to $50 million and finished near $100 million (roughly a 4x overrun that nearly toppled the government of the day), yet CP is worth about $50 billion today (before the Kansas City Southern merger).
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A century-scale case study showing that catastrophic near-term cost overruns on nation-building infrastructure can still be validated many times over by long-run asset value — the argument for tolerating overruns on state-backed megaprojects.
insights.quote: If you look at the railway today, before the Kansas City merger, CP is worth $50 billion. They spent a hundred million. It was 100 years ago, but they spent 100 million, but the value of it today is 50 billion.

insights.claim: MacGregor built the Sturgeon Refinery as a hydrogen-addition refinery rather than a cheaper, more common coker specifically to avoid converting about 15% of every barrel of bitumen into low-value petroleum coke, choosing instead to convert the full barrel into finished products.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Refinery configuration choice (hydrogen-addition vs. coker) is a direct capex-vs-yield tradeoff that determines both economic output and environmental externality — a screening factor for evaluating bitumen upgrading projects.
insights.quote: I I thought that made economic sense.

insights.claim: MacGregor states petroleum coke exported from coker refineries concentrates all the sulfur and metals (like vanadium) from the original bitumen barrel, and that this coke is currently burned as cheap fuel mainly in China and India (with China starting to tighten regulations), causing acid rain and vanadium oxide pollution whose health effects he says are not well understood.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Exporting raw/coker-processed bitumen effectively exports Canada's emissions and pollution liability overseas to jurisdictions with weaker environmental controls — an ESG/externality argument for domestic upgrading over raw export.
insights.quote: The problem with the coke is everything bad in the barrel of bumen ends up in the coke... you're getting acid rain and you're getting a bunch of venadium metal oxides that no one knows, I think, what the effects of that are.

insights.claim: MacGregor says Alberta consumes roughly 600,000-700,000 barrels per day of diluent to make bitumen pipeline-transportable, with about two-thirds produced domestically and one-third imported from the US on import pipelines that are already running at capacity, and that when diluted bitumen is exported (e.g., via Trans Mountain), the exported diluent tightens supply and widens the heavy-light price differential.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Diluent supply is a binding, near-capacity constraint on bitumen export volumes and a direct lever on the heavy-light crude price differential — worth tracking as an indicator ahead of new oil sands production or export capacity additions.
insights.quote: We use about I think about 6 or 700,000 barrels a day of dilluent in Alberta currently... the import pipelines are both running at capacity.

insights.claim: MacGregor's core diversification thesis is that Canada should stop shipping raw bitumen (diluted with light oil, which inflates shipped volume by roughly 30-50%) and instead capture the margin by refining it domestically into finished products like diesel, arguing the best jobs and most retained value come from conversion/processing rather than extraction.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Frames domestic refining capacity as a direct economic-diversification and jobs lever for Canada, not just an environmental play — relevant to any policy or investment debate on Canadian energy value-add versus raw export.
insights.quote: We waste a lot of the potential value in those materials when we ship them and the longer we ship them the more value we sacrifice. So I think we should be making finished goods wherever possible.

insights.claim: MacGregor states the oil sands' true recoverable resource is far larger than commonly cited: while Alberta's counted/proven reserves are about 180-190 billion barrels (a 75-year reserve life at current production), there is an additional 1.7 trillion barrels of bitumen sitting between the SAGD (deep, steam-extracted) and mining (surface) zones that current extraction methods haven't yet unlocked but that industry expects to eventually recover, requiring continued large-diameter pipeline capacity.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: If accurate, the true long-run oil sands resource base is roughly 9x the commonly cited proven-reserve figure — a bullish long-horizon signal for Alberta pipeline and upgrading capacity investment that isn't captured in standard reserve-life statistics.
insights.quote: Right now there's 1.7 trillion between those two places. We'll figure out how to get it out of there... It's like the biggest reserve on the planet. It's sitting there.

themes.theme: The Gasifier Burner Crisis: A First-of-a-Kind Failure and In-House Fix

insights.claim: The Sturgeon Refinery's gasifier — the unit that converts heavy residual bitumen bottoms and liquid oxygen into hydrogen and pure CO2 — relied on a burner from a licensed German technology supplier (with roots dating to WWII-era German hydrogenation processes) that was designed to last a couple thousand hours but failed after only 40 hours at startup, halting hydrogen production and effectively idling the entire $12 billion refinery.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A textbook illustration of single-point-of-failure risk in first-of-a-kind process technology sourced from an outside licensor — a due-diligence flag for any megaproject relying on unproven or externally-licensed critical components.
insights.quote: The burner is supposed to last a couple of thousand hours... when we start the thing up, the burner lasts 40 hours... you just wasted $12 billion.

insights.claim: With the gasifier down, the refinery could only run on light oil feedstock at a loss, uneconomically, just to keep the workforce occupied, while MacGregor faced sustained negative press coverage during the failure period.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Illustrates the real cash-burn and reputational cost of a critical-path technology failure on a fully capitalized megaproject before revenue ramp.
insights.quote: We ran the refinery on light oil so we can run it but it's not economic. It's just keeping the people busy until we can get it to be economic.

insights.claim: After failing to find any outside vendor able to solve the burner problem, MacGregor assembled an internal team of about six or seven top engineers (computational, heat-transfer specialists) alongside a master welder, and solved the failure entirely in-house in 279 days, spending roughly $12 million on finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation work.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Shows that critical-path failures in first-of-a-kind energy infrastructure can be solved faster and more cheaply in-house with concentrated top talent than by waiting on an original equipment licensor — a case study relevant to any project team facing a vendor-caused technology failure.
insights.quote: So then we'd say to the computer guys, go back and do some more work because this isn't going to work. And eventually we got to a place where he's nodded his head and then he took it on... It was as close to people like me can get to the Manhattan project as ever existed in my life.

insights.claim: The redesigned burner required the water-cooling jacket gap to be held to within a tenth of a millimeter, but the welding process used to assemble it caused about 6mm (±1mm) of shrinkage, so the fix depended on one expert welder's ability to track and compensate for shrinkage during welding — a technique described as not fully transferable to another welder.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Highlights that some critical manufacturing solutions in megaprojects rest on individual tacit craft skill rather than fully documented, repeatable process — a risk factor (key-person dependency) worth flagging for operational continuity.
insights.quote: He'll weld a little bit here and then he welds a little bit over there... he can paint the Mona Lisa, but if you give anybody else the drawings, they're going to look like a paint by numbers.

insights.claim: The redesigned gasifier burners now last between 8,000 and 10,000 operating hours, versus the original 40 hours — a roughly 200x-250x reliability improvement — though MacGregor notes the ultimate lifespan is still not fully known.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Quantifies the magnitude of the engineering turnaround and suggests the fix is durable and economically viable long-term, not a stopgap.
insights.quote: I think we get between 8,000 and 10,000 hours out of a burner now that used to last 40 hours.

themes.theme: Small Modular Reactors: A Contrarian Skeptic's View

insights.claim: MacGregor argues small modular reactors (SMRs) don't make economic sense because most operating overhead — safety staff, security guards, fencing, waste handling — doesn't scale down proportionally with reactor size, so factory-built repeatability might only save around 20% on cost while the underlying scale economics still favor large reactors.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the mainstream SMR investment thesis (factory learning curves driving cost down) from an experienced megaproject builder — worth weighing against SMR proponents' cost claims, especially the overhead/fixed-cost components of nuclear opex.
insights.quote: Small doesn't make sense to me. This does not make sense. It never made sense to me from the start... I just think bigger the better if you're building these things.

insights.claim: MacGregor is skeptical of deploying SMRs in small or remote communities, arguing that if a community can't reliably operate a water treatment plant, it's unrealistic to expect it to safely operate a nuclear reactor.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Raises an operational-capacity objection to distributed/remote SMR deployment models that is separate from the pure cost argument — relevant to remote/off-grid and mining-site SMR business cases.
insights.quote: Who runs them when you put... we can't run a water plant in some of these communities. We're going to put a small modular reactor there. Like, I don't know. That doesn't solve for me.

insights.claim: MacGregor says it typically takes about two turnaround cycles and roughly five years of operation before a first-of-a-kind megaproject facility like the Sturgeon Refinery is fully understood and starts running smoothly, after which incremental engineering safety margins built into thousands of individual pieces of equipment compound into meaningful extra capacity.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic timeline expectation (~5 years, 2 turnarounds) for any first-of-a-kind industrial facility to reach steady-state performance — useful for modeling ramp-up curves in project finance.
insights.quote: It takes you about two turnarounds and about five years before you know how to run it and then all of a sudden magically it starts running really well.

insights.claim: The Sturgeon Refinery, now operated by CNRL (described by MacGregor as the preeminent operator of this type of asset), is running about 15% above its original design capacity because engineers conservatively oversized many of its roughly 7,000 major equipment components during design.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A concrete example of how conservative first-of-a-kind engineering margins can translate into upside capacity once operations mature — a positive long-run economics signal for the asset and its current operator CNRL.
insights.quote: It's running now above about 15% above design... it's printing money right now and it'll do so for the next hundred years.

themes.theme: "Chicken AI": Operator Intuition Over Data Lakes

insights.claim: MacGregor's current venture, which he calls 'chicken AI,' rejects the standard approach of mining large repurposed 'data lakes' for statistical patterns (which he says usually yields little useful signal), instead training models on the subjective sensory judgment of experienced human operators — capturing sound, vibration, temperature, and visual cues alongside the operator's own real-time assessment of whether something is going wrong.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: An alternative, expert-in-the-loop AI training paradigm for industrial predictive maintenance that claims faster, higher-signal results than brute-force data mining — relevant to anyone evaluating industrial AI/predictive-maintenance approaches or vendors.
insights.quote: We've decided that the subjective information in the operator's brain is a substitute for the data that you need to train the model... it's amazing how often they can predict some really complicated problem in the process by the senses that they have if they're experienced.

insights.claim: MacGregor characterizes the conventional 'data lake' AI approach as mindless statistical search through data collected for unrelated purposes, often turning up little of value ('a half a needle'), positioning his operator-sensory approach as both faster and more reliable.
insights.speaker: Ian MacGregor
insights.so_what: A critique of the industry-standard big-data-first approach to industrial AI that reframes domain-expert tacit knowledge as a higher-value training signal than raw historical sensor logs.
insights.quote: I got it, they call it a data lake and then I mindlessly statistically search through this haystack to find something of interest and most often there isn't anything in there or maybe there's a half a needle or something like that.
